summary.title: Why indemnification is hard to picture
points: Claims are rare and land on a different desk, so negotiators rarely see their clauses operate.
The module's spine is the third-party claim lifecycle: letter, notice, control, settlement, money.
Caps, survival periods and consent rights are machinery that decides how that lifecycle plays out.
Much of indemnity negotiation is really about price: residual risk has a value.

exercises.scenario: A colleague says the cap is 'just a number we'll never use'.

questions.prompt: What does the module say a cap really is?
options: A formality that courts usually ignore
The amount the buyer is guaranteed to recover on any claim, whatever happens
The point where the payer stops caring about the outcome
A figure set by the insurer, not the parties
questions.explanation: Above the cap, the downside falls on the other party, even if the payer still controls the litigation.

questions.prompt: A buyer pushes the cap from 10% to 20% of deal value. What is really happening?
options: A change that only matters for fraud claims
The buyer is buying risk protection that has a price
A standard step that sellers must accept
A purely legal point about wording, with no real commercial value attached
questions.explanation: Residual risk could equally be reflected in the headline price.

exercises.scenario: Why do negotiators often misjudge which terms matter?

questions.prompt: What's the structural reason?
options: Indemnity clauses are too short to matter
Lawyers deliberately hide the key terms
Courts rewrite most indemnities after the fact, so the drafting rarely matters
They rarely see a claim, and when one arrives someone else handles it
questions.explanation: The feedback loop is weak: the negotiator rarely learns whether the number mattered.

questions.prompt: What does a survival period mean in practice?
options: When an undiscovered problem becomes permanently yours
How long the seller must keep its insurance
The date the purchase price is finally paid
The deadline by which the seller must disclose every known risk to the buyer
questions.explanation: After expiry, a breach nobody discovered stays with the buyer.

summary.title: Representations and warranties
points: Representation: a statement of fact. Warranty: a promise it's true, with a remedy. Covenant: a promise about future conduct.
A knowledge qualifier turns 'it's true' into 'we're not aware it's false': a large risk transfer in four words.
Ask whose knowledge, actual or constructive, and whether it's defined.
A materiality scrape ignores materiality when measuring loss; a double scrape also for finding breach.
Disclosure schedules are a second risk negotiation, often done late and read carelessly.

exercises.scenario: The seller proposes adding 'to the seller's knowledge' to the litigation representation.

questions.prompt: What does the buyer give up?
options: Nothing, since knowledge is always presumed
The right to rely on the disclosure schedules
Protection against anything the seller genuinely didn't know
Only protection against deliberate fraud by the seller's senior management
questions.explanation: Everything the seller didn't know becomes the buyer's problem.

questions.prompt: Which counter-proposal does the module value highly?
options: Naming the individuals and saying actual or constructive knowledge
Raising the general cap by two percentage points to compensate the buyer
Deleting the disclosure schedules altogether
Adding 'in all material respects' as well
questions.explanation: A defined knowledge standard is worth more than a few extra points on the cap.

exercises.scenario: A rep says 'in all material respects', and the agreement has a single materiality scrape.

questions.prompt: What does the single scrape do?
options: Deletes the representation entirely
Ignores materiality when measuring the loss, not when finding a breach
Removes materiality both for finding a breach and for measuring the loss
Applies only to fundamental representations
questions.explanation: A double scrape would also remove it for deciding whether a breach occurred.

questions.prompt: Why should a buyer read the disclosure schedules as closely as the reps?
options: Schedules can't affect indemnity claims
Schedules are only reviewed by the insurer and don't affect the indemnity at all
Schedules override the governing law clause
Anything properly disclosed is carved out of the representation
questions.explanation: Schedules are a second negotiation about risk, conducted in a spreadsheet.

summary.title: Anatomy of the clause
points: Six questions: who, what losses, what trigger, what procedure, what limits, what other remedies excluded.
Indemnify reimburses after the fact; defend arises when the claim is asserted, even if it fails.
The definition of loss (fees, settlements, diminution in value) is a live negotiation dressed as boilerplate.
Specific indemnities for known risks usually sit outside cap, basket and sometimes survival.
Exclusive remedy stops parties escaping the limits through tort claims; fraud is the usual carve-out.

exercises.scenario: A claim against the buyer is defeated after 14 months of litigation. The seller says it owes nothing.

questions.prompt: Which obligation could still make the seller pay?
options: The hold harmless wording, which only applies after judgment
A duty to defend, owed from when the claim was asserted
The indemnity, which is triggered even by failed claims
The exclusive remedy clause, which covers all costs
questions.explanation: A defense can be owed on a claim that ultimately fails.

questions.prompt: A recall is already under way at signing. How is it usually handled?
options: A specific indemnity, outside the general cap and basket
Covered by the general cap like any other risk
Excluded as a known issue under the exclusive remedy clause, so nobody pays
Disclosed and therefore left with the buyer
questions.explanation: A known, sizeable risk shouldn't compete with unknown risks for space under a shared cap.

exercises.scenario: The buyer's counsel wants to sue for misrepresentation to escape the cap.

questions.prompt: What usually blocks this?
options: The survival period
The disclosure schedules
An exclusive remedy clause
The de minimis threshold
questions.explanation: Indemnification is the sole recourse, except usually for fraud.

questions.prompt: Why does the definition of 'fraud' in the carve-out matter?
options: It determines the size of the escrow
It decides which court hears the dispute
It sets the length of the survival period for all general representations
Too narrow and it's unreachable; too broad and it swallows the exclusivity
questions.explanation: The scope of the fraud carve-out repays careful reading.

summary.title: Direct claims and third-party claims
points: Direct claim: one party against the other; nothing external to defend.
Third-party claim: an outsider sues; someone must run a live proceeding.
Notice, control, cooperation and consent machinery only makes sense for third-party claims.
Direct-claim notice requiring a loss estimate can kill a claim found late; use 'to the extent then determinable'.
In pharma, one set of facts often creates both claim types, with separate deadlines.

exercises.scenario: In month 20 of a 24-month survival period, the buyer finds a compliance breach but can't size the loss yet.

questions.prompt: What protects the buyer best?
options: Treating it as a third-party claim, which gives the buyer extra time to notify
Waiting until the loss is known, then serving notice
Asking the seller to agree an extension informally
A clause allowing an estimate 'to the extent then determinable'
questions.explanation: It preserves the claim without demanding a number that doesn't exist yet.

questions.prompt: Which machinery has no application to this direct claim?
options: The survival period and the cap
Dispute resolution under the agreement
Control of defense and consent to settle
Notice and a response period
questions.explanation: There's no external proceeding to defend.

exercises.scenario: A patient sues the acquired business, and the seller had hidden a safety signal.

questions.prompt: How many claim paths are open?
options: One: only the patient's claim matters, because product liability absorbs the rest
Two: a third-party claim and a direct claim for breach of a rep
None, because product liability is excluded
One: only the direct claim against the seller
questions.explanation: Same facts, two procedures, two sets of deadlines.

questions.prompt: What's the risk in that situation?
options: Meeting one procedure's deadlines while missing the other's
The direct claim must wait for the trial
The cap doubles because two claims exist
The patient's claim automatically cancels the buyer's direct claim on the same facts
questions.explanation: Overlooking one path can leave part of the exposure unrecovered.

summary.title: The first thirty days
points: Read notice for timing, content and consequence: is notice a condition precedent?
Late notice usually defeats a claim only to the extent of prejudice, unless it's a condition precedent.
Two clocks: notice to the counterparty and to the insurer. The insurance clock is less forgiving.
Issue a litigation hold early; spoliation weakens the defense and creates real prejudice.
Don't engage the claimant substantively, and don't wait for certainty before notifying.

exercises.scenario: A claim letter arrives on Monday. Legal plans to notify the seller this week and the broker 'once it looks serious'.

questions.prompt: What's the biggest risk in that plan?
options: Losing insurance coverage through late notice to the insurer
Breaching the seller's consent-to-settle right
Waiving privilege by telling the broker
Losing the indemnity through a late contractual notice to the seller this week
questions.explanation: Under a claims-made policy, notice within the period is what makes coverage exist.

questions.prompt: A manager drafts a friendly reply to the claimant explaining what happened. Advice?
options: Send it only if it avoids admitting fault
Send it quickly to show good faith
Don't send it before internal alignment
Send it, but copy the seller
questions.explanation: A well-meant reply can prejudice both the defense and coverage.

exercises.scenario: The contract says notice is a 'condition precedent' to indemnification.

questions.prompt: What changes?
options: The survival period is extended
A missed deadline can mean the indemnity never arises
Nothing changes; the seller must still show it was prejudiced by the delay
The insurer takes over the notice
questions.explanation: The word 'condition' turns an arguable slip into a fatal one.

questions.prompt: How can a poor litigation hold hurt the indemnity claim?
options: It cancels the duty to defend automatically
It doubles the basket for the claim
It moves control of defense to the insurer and cancels the seller's election right
It creates real prejudice, turning a notice defect into a defense for the payer
questions.explanation: Spoliation findings travel and weaken the indemnified party's position.

summary.title: Control of defense
points: Control decides counsel, strategy, concessions and settlement: whether the case is run to minimise payout or protect a business.
The payer usually has 15–30 days to elect; silence usually means declining.
Counsel 'reasonably satisfactory' and a right to participate at own expense are standard.
Control should revert for conflicts, non-monetary relief, criminal or regulatory matters, and claims above the cap.
An insurer may appoint panel counsel, and may defend under a reservation of rights.

exercises.scenario: A competitor seeks an injunction to take the buyer's product off the market. The seller wants to run the defense.

questions.prompt: Which carve-out should return control to the buyer?
options: Fraud by the seller
Claims under the basket
Non-monetary relief
Claims below the de minimis
questions.explanation: The party that must live with the outcome should be running it.

questions.prompt: A claim worth 30 is defended by a seller with 10 left under the cap. What's the problem?
options: Above 10, the seller has no stake, so its incentive to fight disappears
The insurer automatically takes control
The seller must now pay the full 30 regardless of the cap, because it chose to defend
The claim becomes a direct claim
questions.explanation: The sharpest, most often omitted carve-out.

exercises.scenario: The contract says the seller picks counsel; the seller's insurer says it appoints from its panel.

questions.prompt: Who usually decides in practice?
options: The buyer, as the party being sued
The insurer, because it's funding the defense
The seller, because the contract it negotiated says so and the contract prevails
The court, on application by either side
questions.explanation: The policy can override what the parties negotiated.

questions.prompt: Why is defense under a reservation of rights awkward?
options: The insured must pay all costs upfront
The claimant can see the insurer's file
The insurer has already accepted the claim in full, so counsel has no conflict at all
Appointed counsel reports to a party that may later deny coverage
questions.explanation: Facts developed in the defense can inform the coverage decision.

summary.title: Consent to settle
points: Different exposure creates different optimal settlements: the disagreement is structural.
Near the cap, the payer wants to settle at any figure below it.
A cheap settlement with an admission can be commercially disastrous for the operator.
Payer can't settle without consent for admissions, non-monetary terms, no full release or above-cap amounts; the indemnified party can't settle alone at all.
Insurers add a third consent; a hammer clause caps the insurer at its recommended figure.

exercises.scenario: The seller, controlling the defense, proposes settling at 4 with an admission of a safety defect.

questions.prompt: Can the buyer block it?
options: Usually yes: settlements with an admission need its consent
No: once it elects to defend, the controlling party settles freely on any terms
Only if the insurer also objects
Only if the amount exceeds the cap
questions.explanation: Admissions are one of the standard consent triggers.

questions.prompt: Why might the buyer refuse even though 4 is cheap?
options: Because the seller pays nothing
Because 4 is above the basket, so the buyer would have to fund part of it itself
Because admissions are illegal in pharma
The admission will be cited in every later claim and to the regulator
questions.explanation: The payer sees a number; the operator sees a document.

exercises.scenario: The insurer recommends settling at 5; the insured wants to fight. The policy has a hard hammer clause.

questions.prompt: What happens?
options: The insurer must keep funding the defense in full
The insurer pays at most 5 plus defense costs so far
The insured loses all coverage immediately
The insurer and insured split all further costs 70/30 under the hard hammer clause
questions.explanation: The insured can fight on, at its own expense from that point.

questions.prompt: What happens if the indemnified party settles alone without consent?
options: The cap is reduced by half
The payer must reimburse the settlement anyway, as long as the amount was reasonable
It usually forfeits the indemnity for that claim
The settlement becomes void
questions.explanation: The harsher of the two consent rights, and standard.

summary.title: Cooperation, privilege and joint defense
points: Documents and witnesses sit with the indemnified party, so cooperation duties fall mostly on it.
Ask who pays for cooperation: staff time, review and vendor costs.
Sharing privileged material usually waives privilege; common interest can protect it.
Common interest needs a shared legal interest, is fragile if parties become adverse, and varies by jurisdiction.
Insurer cooperation duties are enforced harder; disclosure to an insurer can waive privilege.

exercises.scenario: Seller and buyer are defending a product claim together and want to share candid exposure memos.

questions.prompt: What doctrine lets them share without waiving privilege?
options: Mitigation, if costs are reduced
Common interest, if they share a legal interest
Subrogation, once the insurer pays
Exclusive remedy, as long as the fraud carve-out is excluded from the agreement
questions.explanation: A shared commercial wish for the claim to disappear isn't enough.

questions.prompt: What should a joint defense agreement address above all?
options: The seat of any future arbitration between the two of them over the indemnity
The amount of the general cap
Whether shared material can be used if the parties later fall out
The insurer's panel counsel rates
questions.explanation: The divergence provisions are the ones worth reading.

exercises.scenario: The insurer, defending under a reservation of rights, asks for counsel's frank memo on weaknesses.

questions.prompt: What's the danger?
options: Handing your weaknesses to a party that may deny coverage, and possibly waiving privilege
It breaches the consent-to-settle clause
None; insurers are always within common interest
It ends the reservation of rights automatically
questions.explanation: Ask the question before sending the memo.

questions.prompt: How do consequences differ for failing to cooperate?
options: Both are measured only by prejudice, so a short delay rarely has any consequence
Both void protection automatically
Neither has any real consequence
With the counterparty it's measured by prejudice; with the insurer it can void coverage
questions.explanation: The insurer's sanction is categorical rather than proportionate.

summary.title: Damages
points: Direct, consequential, incidental and punitive damages: the labels aren't settled across jurisdictions.
Excluding 'consequential damages' leaves lost profits arguable; naming them closes it.
Multiple-based damages: an EBITDA overstatement can mean overpayment times the deal multiple.
Liquidated damages must not be penalties (common law); civil law courts often reduce them instead.
Recovery is net of mitigation, insurance proceeds, third-party recoveries and tax benefits.

exercises.scenario: The seller overstated EBITDA by 1m; the buyer paid 8× EBITDA.

questions.prompt: What's the buyer's argument on loss?
options: Its loss is 8m plus punitive damages
Its loss is the overpayment: about 8m
Its loss is the shortfall itself: 1m
It has no loss until it sells the business
questions.explanation: Whoever wins the drafting point moves the indemnity's value by a factor of eight.

questions.prompt: The seller insists on excluding 'damages based on a multiple'. What does that do?
options: Turns the EBITDA claim into a specific indemnity outside the general cap
Doubles the claim to 16m
Removes the cap entirely
Limits the claim to the 1m shortfall
questions.explanation: That's the seller's standard protection.

exercises.scenario: A supply deal excludes 'consequential, indirect and special damages'.

questions.prompt: What's the weakness of that wording?
options: Stacked labels without a definition invite an argument
It only applies to punitive damages
It excludes all damages, including direct ones, so the indemnity is worth nothing
It's unenforceable under every governing law
questions.explanation: Courts don't treat the three identically.

questions.prompt: 'Net of insurance proceeds recoverable' rather than 'received'. Who does it hurt?
options: The indemnifying party, which now pays more because insurance is ignored entirely
The insurer, which loses subrogation
The indemnified party, which must claim on its own policy first
Nobody; the two wordings mean the same
questions.explanation: It affects premiums and future coverage, a cost the payer doesn't bear.

summary.title: Caps, baskets and de minimis
points: De minimis: claims below it are ignored and usually don't count toward the basket.
Without an aggregation clause, many small linked breaches are unrecoverable.
Deductible basket: recover only the excess. Tipping basket: recover from the first unit once crossed.
Caps are tiered: general, fundamental, tax, and uncapped fraud. Ask which cap applies.
Most claims are decided by de minimis, aggregation and basket type, not the cap.

exercises.scenario: Deal 100; de minimis 0.05; basket 1; cap 10. Claims: 0.03, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6.

questions.prompt: What's recovered with a deductible basket?
questions.explanation: 0.03 is ignored; 1.2 aggregate minus the 1.0 basket leaves 0.2.

questions.prompt: And with a tipping basket?
questions.explanation: Once over the threshold, recovery runs from the first unit (still excluding the 0.03).

exercises.scenario: A buyer trades a deductible basket for 2 extra points on the cap.

questions.prompt: What does the module say about that trade?
options: A good trade, because the cap is the biggest number and decides most claims
Almost certainly a bad one: most claims never reach the cap
Neutral, since baskets and caps offset
Good only if fraud is uncapped
questions.explanation: The basket type decides far more claims than the cap.

questions.prompt: Thirty small errors from one faulty compliance process each fall below de minimis.
options: Recoverable only if there's an aggregation clause
Recoverable only under the fraud carve-out, since each error is below de minimis
Always recoverable as one claim
Never recoverable under any clause
questions.explanation: Aggregation lets claims from the same facts count as one.

summary.title: Survival periods
points: General reps survive about 12–24 months: one audit cycle.
Tiered: fundamentals long or indefinite; tax to the assessment period; IP intermediate; specific indemnities until resolved.
A claim notified before expiry should survive until resolved; 'resolved within the period' is a trap.
Notice requiring a loss estimate bites hardest near expiry.
Pharma's latent risks need specific indemnities and insurance, not longer general survival.

exercises.scenario: A 24-month survival clause requires claims to be 'resolved' within the period. A third-party claim is notified in month 18.

questions.prompt: What's the problem?
options: The cap doubles after month 24
The claim may expire before it can realistically be resolved
The claim converts to a direct claim
None; notice alone preserves it, whatever the clause says about resolution
questions.explanation: A survival that requires resolution isn't really a 24-month survival.

questions.prompt: Which wording should the buyer have asked for?
options: All claims survive indefinitely
Claims must be resolved within 36 months, with a single extension allowed
Only fraud claims survive closing
Claims notified before expiry survive until finally resolved
questions.explanation: The period governs when you must raise a claim, not finish it.

exercises.scenario: A buyer is worried about a safety signal that could appear in year four.

questions.prompt: What's the right instrument?
options: A larger general cap
A tipping basket
A specific indemnity or insurance, not the general survival period
A longer general survival of 30 months for every business representation
questions.explanation: General survival is designed around the audit cycle, not pharma latency.

questions.prompt: Why do title representations survive much longer?
options: A title defect goes to whether the buyer got what it paid for
Title is easy to check at closing, so a long period costs the seller nothing
Tax law requires it
Insurers insist on it
questions.explanation: Fundamental reps get long or indefinite survival.

summary.title: Escrow and holdback
points: An indemnity is only as good as the payer's existence and solvency when the claim arrives.
Escrow: neutral agent, release schedule, pending claims retained, interest and fees negotiated.
Holdback: cheaper, but the seller bears the buyer's credit risk and incentives.
If escrow is the exclusive source of recovery, it's the real cap.
R&W insurance often shrinks or removes escrow.

exercises.scenario: The SPA has a 10% cap; the escrow agreement makes a 5% escrow the exclusive source of recovery.

questions.prompt: What's the real cap?
options: Unlimited for fraud only
questions.explanation: A 10% cap backed by a 5% exclusive escrow is a 5% cap with extra steps.

questions.prompt: Where is this point usually decided?
options: In the R&W policy exclusions
In the disclosure schedules
In the governing law clause, which decides how the cap is read
In the escrow agreement, which gets less attention
questions.explanation: It often moves the economics more than the cap negotiation.

exercises.scenario: A private equity seller will wind up its vehicle soon after closing.

questions.prompt: Why does that matter to the buyer?
options: The seller's insurer takes over
There may be nobody to claim against later
Survival periods are suspended
The cap becomes unlimited
questions.explanation: An uncapped indemnity from a dissolved party is worth little.

questions.prompt: A known pending lawsuit needs security. What's common?
options: Using the general escrow for it, since all claims share one pot anyway
A holdback with no release date
A separate escrow released when that matter resolves
Relying on the R&W policy
questions.explanation: It stops a known risk consuming the escrow for unknown ones; R&W excludes known issues.

summary.title: Insurance and R&W insurance
points: Occurrence policies cover events in the period; claims-made cover claims made in the period.
Claims-made needs the right retroactive date and tail cover, especially when the seller dissolves.
Deductible: insurer runs the claim. Self-insured retention: insured runs it until exhausted.
Gaps between seller and buyer programmes need assignment or additional-insured status; watch subrogation.
R&W insurance excludes known issues and often pharma product, regulatory and IP risks.

exercises.scenario: A product sold in 2019 under the seller's claims-made policy, which lapsed at closing, triggers a 2026 claim.

questions.prompt: Is it covered?
options: Not unless tail cover was bought
Yes, because the event was in 2019
Yes, under the buyer's new policy automatically
Only if the claim is below the retention
questions.explanation: Under claims-made, the claim must be made while the policy (or its extended reporting period) is live.

questions.prompt: Which policy type would have covered it as of right?
options: An R&W policy on the acquisition
An occurrence-based policy in force in 2019
A policy with a self-insured retention
A claims-made policy bought by the buyer in 2026 after the claim arrived
questions.explanation: Occurrence policies cover events in the period, whenever the claim arrives.

exercises.scenario: The buyer plans to rely on R&W insurance instead of a seller indemnity in a pharma deal.

questions.prompt: What's the key gap?
options: R&W insurance requires a larger escrow and longer survival than a seller indemnity
R&W policies never pay out
R&W insurance only covers tax
Known issues and often product, regulatory and IP risks are excluded
questions.explanation: It may cover the reps you worry about least.

questions.prompt: Your insurer pays a claim caused by your distribution partner. What might follow?
options: Nothing; once the insurer has paid, the matter is closed for every party
The partner's cap doubles
The insurer pursues the partner through subrogation
Your policy is cancelled
questions.explanation: That's why waivers of subrogation exist.

summary.title: Pharma-specific claims
points: Product liability: latent, multiple claimants, linked to pharmacovigilance failures.
An indemnity allocates risk between the parties; successor liability can still let claimants sue the buyer.
IP claims often seek an injunction, which an indemnity can't fix: control should sit with the buyer.
Infringing others' rights threatens sales; invalidity of acquired rights threatens value.
Regulators act rather than sue; check the 'third-party claim' definition and who handles the regulator.

exercises.scenario: After an asset deal allocating pre-closing liability to the seller, a patient sues the buyer.

questions.prompt: What does the indemnity do?
options: Gives the buyer a right to recover after being sued, defending and paying
Makes the seller the defendant automatically, so the buyer drops out of the case
Transfers the claim to the regulator
Stops the patient suing the buyer
questions.explanation: Indemnities don't bind third parties; successor liability may apply.

questions.prompt: What then decides whether the allocation was real?
options: The patient's choice of court and how quickly the case is heard
The size of the basket
The seller's survival, solvency and security
The buyer's market share
questions.explanation: Back to escrow and security.

exercises.scenario: A regulator suspends a marketing authorisation because of pre-closing conduct.

questions.prompt: What should you check first in the agreement?
options: Whether the basket is deductible
Whether 'third-party claim' captures a regulatory action
Whether the cap includes tax
Whether the escrow earns interest
questions.explanation: Definitions are often drafted around litigation only.

questions.prompt: A pre-closing bribery issue is discovered. What's the tension?
options: The seller can block any disclosure
It's covered by R&W insurance as standard
The buyer must stay silent to protect the indemnity until the seller agrees to disclose
A disclosure duty may conflict with the seller's defense interests
questions.explanation: The regulatory clock runs faster than the indemnity clock.

summary.title: Choice of law
points: Governing law decides how damages, liquidated sums, good faith and ambiguity are treated.
English law: predictable and textual, no general good faith duty. New York: deep M&A case law.
Swiss law: neutral civil law, with good faith and court power to reduce penalties.
Mandatory rules and limitation periods can't be contracted away.
Third-party claims follow their own law, not the contract's.

exercises.scenario: Your SPA is under English law. A patient injured in Germany sues the buyer.

questions.prompt: Which law governs the patient's claim?
options: German law (or the law applicable there), not English law
Whichever law the seller chooses
Swiss law, as a neutral law
English law, as agreed in the SPA, because it binds anyone suing over the product
questions.explanation: The governing law clause only binds the parties to it.

questions.prompt: A clause sets a large stipulated sum for missing a milestone. Under Swiss law, what's likely?
options: The sum is always enforced in full
A court may reduce an excessive sum
The sum converts to a cap
The sum is struck out entirely as a penalty
questions.explanation: Civil law courts tend to reduce rather than void.

exercises.scenario: A party withholds consent to settle. The agreement says 'not unreasonably withheld'.

questions.prompt: Why does the governing law matter here?
options: It doesn't matter; the phrase means exactly the same under every governing law
It decides the size of the basket
It decides which insurer pays
Civil law adds a general good faith duty; English law generally doesn't
questions.explanation: It shapes how a discretion may be exercised.

questions.prompt: Why might a negotiated survival period be undermined?
options: The insurer can override it
Survival periods are always void
Some laws restrict contracting out of statutory limitation
Arbitration ignores survival periods, so they only bind in court proceedings
questions.explanation: Limitation rules can upset a survival period from either direction.

summary.title: Courts or arbitration
points: Arbitration isn't reliably faster or cheaper; it offers neutrality, expertise, confidentiality and enforceable awards.
The cost is finality: errors of law usually can't be appealed.
The seat decides procedural law, supervising courts and where an award can be set aside; the venue is just the place.
Choose institution, number of arbitrators, language, scope and interim relief deliberately.
Avoid pathological clauses; confidentiality must be stated, not assumed.

exercises.scenario: A clause says 'ICC arbitration, seated in Zurich, hearings in Dubai'.

questions.prompt: Which courts can set the award aside?
options: Any court where assets sit
The Swiss courts
The Dubai courts
The ICC court in Paris
questions.explanation: Only the courts of the seat can annul an award.

questions.prompt: A three-member ICC tribunal for every dispute, including small ones. Effect?
options: Appeals become available
Costs fall because ICC is administered and sets the fees
Small claims are resolved faster
Small claims become uneconomic to pursue
questions.explanation: A procedural choice with a substantive outcome; consider a sole arbitrator below a threshold.

exercises.scenario: A dispute clause provides for arbitration and gives exclusive jurisdiction to the Geneva courts.

questions.prompt: What's the problem?
options: It's pathological: a dispute about the dispute
It makes the award unenforceable abroad automatically
It removes the governing law
None; parties can choose both
questions.explanation: Contradictory clauses cost months and fees before the merits.

questions.prompt: Your dispute will involve safety data. What should the clause do?
options: Rely on arbitration being confidential by default
Choose litigation for confidentiality
State confidentiality expressly
Use an ad hoc tribunal
questions.explanation: The default is less protective than most assume.

summary.title: Enforcement across borders
points: Arbitral awards travel under a widely ratified convention; court judgments mostly don't outside regional frameworks.
Enforcement can be refused only on narrow grounds; public policy is the most variable.
Setting aside happens at the seat; resisting enforcement happens where assets are.
You enforce where the assets are; ask where they are at signing.
States may waive immunity from jurisdiction but not from execution; structure to avoid needing enforcement.

exercises.scenario: Your distributor in the Gulf has assets only at home. You're choosing between English courts and arbitration.

questions.prompt: What usually decides it?
options: Arbitration, because the award is far easier to enforce there
English courts, because English judgments are enforced everywhere by treaty
Neither; enforcement doesn't depend on forum
English courts, because they're faster
questions.explanation: Enforceability, not speed or cost, should decide.

questions.prompt: What's even better than a good enforcement clause?
options: A longer survival period and a higher cap to compensate for the enforcement risk
A higher cap
Security that avoids enforcement: guarantee, letter of credit or escrow
A tipping basket
questions.explanation: Convert an enforcement problem into a documentation problem.

exercises.scenario: A ministry of health signed an arbitration clause and lost. Its assets are used for public functions.

questions.prompt: Can you seize them?
options: No: states can never be sued
Yes, but only at the seat
Yes: agreeing to arbitrate waives all immunity, including immunity from execution
Not necessarily: immunity from execution may still apply
questions.explanation: Waiving jurisdictional immunity isn't waiving immunity from execution.

questions.prompt: An award is refused enforcement in one country. What then?
options: It's automatically set aside at the seat
It may still be enforced elsewhere
It's void everywhere
It must be re-heard on the merits
questions.explanation: Only annulment at the seat usually kills it everywhere.

summary.title: Building judgment
points: Attention and consequence are badly correlated: the cap gets debated, the basket and escrow decide.
Experienced people ask different first questions: basket, escrow exclusivity, R&W exclusions, assets, notice conditions.
Feedback is weak: claims arrive years later, handled by someone else.
Close the loop on purpose: read every package, post-mortem claims, read judgments.
Ask 'what would actually happen?', not 'is this clause acceptable?'

exercises.scenario: You have 20 minutes before a negotiation call on a draft SPA.

questions.prompt: Which check comes first, according to the module?
options: The basket type, before the cap
The parties' names and addresses
The headline cap percentage
The definition of fraud
questions.explanation: Terms that look like mechanics often decide outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which document should you also open?
options: The NDA
The board minutes
The press release
The escrow agreement
questions.explanation: Exclusivity there can override the cap.

exercises.scenario: A claim hit a deal your colleague negotiated three years ago.

questions.prompt: What's the most valuable thing to do with it?
options: Ask the insurer for its view only
Count how many clauses were negotiated
Post-mortem which provisions actually decided the outcome
File it with litigation and move on, since the negotiator can't change it now
questions.explanation: This is the only direct feedback available, and it's routinely wasted.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why does the module call an indemnity 'a bet'?
questions.modelAnswer: Because it depends, years in advance, on the counterparty still existing, being solvent and willing to pay, under a law and in a forum that may not have been chosen carefully, and secured by whatever amount was negotiated in a side document. So the question is what would actually happen, not whether the clause reads well.

summary.title: Foundations
points: Indemnity is machinery for a claim lifecycle; negotiators rarely see it operate.
Qualifiers (knowledge, materiality) and schedules decide what a rep actually protects.
Indemnify, defend and hold harmless arise at different moments.
Specific indemnities handle known risks; exclusive remedy keeps the limits intact.

exercises.scenario: You're buying a generics portfolio. A known patent suit is pending, and the seller wants broad knowledge qualifiers.

questions.prompt: How should the known patent suit be handled?
options: Disclosed, so it becomes the buyer's risk
A specific indemnity outside the general cap and basket
Ignored, because a buy-side R&W policy will cover the pending patent suit
Included in the general cap like other risks
questions.explanation: A known risk shouldn't compete with unknown ones under a shared cap.

questions.prompt: Which knowledge qualifier is least bad for the buyer?
options: Actual knowledge of named people after reasonable enquiry
Undefined 'knowledge' of the company
Knowledge of anyone in management, at any time before or after signing
Knowledge as of the signing date only
questions.explanation: Defined, named, and with an enquiry element.

questions.prompt: Why does the buyer want an exclusive remedy clause less than the seller does?
options: It extends the survival period
It stops the buyer escaping the caps through tort claims
It removes the seller's fraud carve-out and so protects the buyer's recovery
It increases the basket
questions.explanation: Exclusivity protects the negotiated limits, which mostly help the seller.

exercises.scenario: Link the foundations to price.

questions.prompt: A seller offers a lower price in exchange for a 5% cap and knowledge qualifiers. What's the right framing?
options: A standard request with no economic value
A purely legal point to reject on principle, because caps aren't priced
A commercial trade of residual risk for price
A sign of fraud by the seller
questions.explanation: Indemnity negotiation is largely about price.

questions.prompt: Which obligation can cost money even if the claim fails?
options: Exclusive remedy
Hold harmless (in every court)
Indemnify
Defend
questions.explanation: Defense costs accrue while the claim is live.

questions.prompt: In your own words: what is the difference between a single and a double materiality scrape?
questions.modelAnswer: A single scrape ignores materiality qualifiers only when calculating the loss once a breach is found. A double scrape also ignores them when deciding whether a breach happened at all, so even small inaccuracies count as breaches.

summary.title: The third-party claim machine
points: Direct and third-party claims need different procedures; pharma facts often trigger both.
Two notice clocks run at once; the insurer's is stricter. Watch condition-precedent wording.
Control of defense should revert for conflicts, injunctions, regulatory matters and above-cap claims.
Consent rights look symmetric but favour whoever controls the defense; insurers add a third veto.
Cooperation and privilege need a joint defense agreement and care with insurers.

exercises.scenario: Month 1 of a product claim worth well above the seller's cap. The seller elects to defend; its insurer appoints panel counsel under a reservation of rights.

questions.prompt: Which carve-out lets the buyer take back control?
options: Claims exceeding the cap
Claims below de minimis
Direct claims
Claims under a tipping basket
questions.explanation: The seller has no stake above the cap.

questions.prompt: The buyer wants to share an internal root-cause analysis with the insurer. First question?
options: Does it fit the escrow agreement?
Has the survival period started?
Is the basket deductible or tipping, and does the insurer need to know that?
Could this waive privilege or help the insurer deny cover?
questions.explanation: The insurer has already signalled possible adversity.

questions.prompt: The insurer recommends settling; the buyer refuses. What clause decides the cost?
options: The de minimis clause
The hammer clause
The exclusive remedy clause
The governing law clause
questions.explanation: It caps the insurer's liability at the recommended figure plus costs.

exercises.scenario: Trace how one early mistake damages later stages.

questions.prompt: Late notice to the insurer in week 1 affects what later?
options: Nothing, if the contract notice was on time
Only the seller's indemnity, not insurance, because the policy has no notice rule
Coverage, and so who funds the defense and any settlement
Only the governing law
questions.explanation: The insurance clock is less forgiving than the contractual one.

questions.prompt: A poor litigation hold in week 1 helps whom later?
options: The buyer, which gets more time to notify because the facts are now unclear
The insurer, which must then pay more
Nobody; holds are a formality
The payer, which can argue it was prejudiced
questions.explanation: Spoliation turns a technical defect into real prejudice.

questions.prompt: Why does the party with most to lose often have least settlement leverage?
options: The controlling party shapes the offer, and refusal risks an 'unreasonable withholding' fight
Because insurers favour the indemnified party
Because consent rights are always one-sided by law
Because direct claims can't settle
questions.explanation: Symmetric in form, asymmetric in effect.

summary.title: The financial architecture
points: Damages wording (lost profits, multiples) can move recovery by a factor of eight.
De minimis, aggregation and basket type decide most claims; the cap decides few.
Survival: notified-then-survives, tiered periods, and pharma latency handled by other tools.
Escrow exclusivity can be the real cap; holdback shifts credit risk to the seller.
Insurance: occurrence vs claims-made, tail cover, retentions, R&W exclusions.

exercises.scenario: A buyer gets a 15% cap, a deductible basket of 1%, a 12-month survival requiring resolution, a 3% exclusive escrow, and a damages clause excluding multiples.

questions.prompt: What's the effective maximum recovery?
options: 15%, the negotiated cap
3%, because the escrow is exclusive
18%, cap plus escrow
Unlimited, because fraud is uncapped
questions.explanation: Exclusivity overrides the cap.

questions.prompt: Which term most threatens a third-party claim notified in month 10?
options: The 15% cap
The deductible basket
Survival requiring resolution within 12 months
Excluding multiple-based damages
questions.explanation: A long-running claim can't be resolved in two months.

questions.prompt: If EBITDA was overstated, what does the multiples exclusion do?
options: Raises recovery to the overpayment, since the buyer paid a multiple of EBITDA
Limits recovery to the shortfall, not the overpayment
Has no effect on EBITDA claims
Turns it into a fraud claim
questions.explanation: The seller has won the multiple fight.

exercises.scenario: The buyer adds buy-side R&W insurance.

questions.prompt: What typically changes?
options: The basket becomes tipping by law
Larger escrow and longer survival, because the insurer demands extra security
No change to the package
Smaller caps, shorter survival and minimal escrow
questions.explanation: The security function moves to the insurer.

questions.prompt: What still needs a seller indemnity?
options: Known issues found in diligence
Arithmetic errors in accounts
Breaches of title reps
Unknown breaches of general reps
questions.explanation: R&W policies exclude known issues.

questions.prompt: In your own words: why does the basket type often matter more than the cap?
questions.modelAnswer: Most claims are far smaller than the cap. Whether a claim pays the excess only (deductible) or everything once the threshold is crossed (tipping) changes recovery on almost every claim, sometimes by a factor of six, while the cap only bites on the rare very large claim.

summary.title: Pharma claims, law and forum
points: Product liability, IP and regulatory claims behave differently; size the package to each.
Indemnities don't stop third parties suing; successor liability may apply.
Governing law decides interpretation; third-party claims follow their own law.
Forum: the seat matters most; arbitration trades appeal rights for enforceable awards.
Enforcement follows assets; secure the deal so you never need to enforce.

exercises.scenario: A Swiss licensor out-licenses to a Saudi state-owned distributor. Disputes: 'English courts, English law'.

questions.prompt: What's the biggest practical problem?
options: English law can't govern a licence
Saudi law will govern the contract anyway, so the English law clause is void
An English judgment may be hard to enforce where the assets are
English courts can't hear licensing disputes
questions.explanation: Choose a forum by where you'd need to enforce.

questions.prompt: What would improve the position most?
options: Switching to Swiss courts, which enforce everywhere in the Gulf by treaty
Adding a tipping basket
Raising the cap
Arbitration with a sound seat, an immunity waiver and security
questions.explanation: Both jurisdiction and execution immunity need waiving, and security avoids enforcement.

questions.prompt: The product is withdrawn by the Saudi regulator for pre-closing conduct. What's the first contract check?
options: Whether 'third-party claim' covers regulatory action
Whether the hammer clause applies
Whether the basket is deductible
Whether the escrow earns interest
questions.explanation: Regulators act; they don't sue.

exercises.scenario: Connect law, forum and enforcement.

questions.prompt: Why should governing law and forum be decided separately?
options: Forum always follows the governing law
Only the forum affects damages
Law decides how the contract is read; forum decides who reads it and whether the result travels
They're legally the same choice
questions.explanation: Combining them is how parties pick a forum by accident.

questions.prompt: An IP claimant seeks an injunction against the buyer's product. Who should control the defense?
options: The insurer, under its panel
The buyer, because non-monetary relief affects its business
The tribunal, by appointment
The seller, because it pays and the contract usually gives it control
questions.explanation: An indemnity can't make good an injunction.

questions.prompt: An award is annulled at the seat. What usually follows?
options: It can't be enforced elsewhere
It is re-heard at the venue
It can still be enforced everywhere
It converts into a court judgment
questions.explanation: Annulment at the seat destroys the award at source.

summary.title: Indemnification: the whole picture
points: An indemnity is a bet on a counterparty's existence, solvency and willingness to pay, years ahead.
The claim lifecycle (notice, control, consent, cooperation) runs alongside an insurer's stricter rules.
Money is decided by damages wording, de minimis, aggregation, basket type, escrow exclusivity and the right cap.
Pharma risks are latent, multiple and regulatory; use specific indemnities and insurance.
Governing law, seat and asset location decide whether a win becomes money.
Attention and consequence are badly correlated: check the mechanics first.

exercises.scenario: You're reviewing your company's out-licensing template for MENA partners before the next negotiation.

questions.prompt: Which three terms deserve the first look?
options: Price, volume and term only
Recitals, definitions and signature blocks
Basket type, escrow exclusivity and the dispute clause
The cap first, then the cap for fundamentals, then the cap for tax
questions.explanation: The terms that look like mechanics decide outcomes.

questions.prompt: A partner proposes 'courts of the partner's home country, home law'. What's your main concern?
options: Only the partner's insurance
Only the length of the survival period and whether it starts at signing or closing
Only the court's language
Whether a judgment could be enforced and how the law reads the clauses
questions.explanation: Law, forum and enforcement are linked but separate questions.

questions.prompt: Which notice wording should be in every template?
options: Notice is only needed for third-party claims
Claims may be notified with a loss estimate 'to the extent then determinable'
Notice is a condition precedent to any claim
Notice must include a final loss figure
questions.explanation: It preserves claims found late in the survival period.

exercises.scenario: A third-party product claim arrives two years after closing on a deal you negotiated.

questions.prompt: Which provision decides who runs the defense?
options: The materiality scrape
Control of defense, as limited by the insurer's rights
The disclosure schedules
The exclusive remedy clause, which decides who runs any proceeding
questions.explanation: The policy can override the contract's allocation.

questions.prompt: The claim exceeds the cap. What follows across the package?
options: The claim converts to a direct claim
The seller must keep paying in full
The cap automatically doubles
Control should revert, the payer may push to settle at the cap, and the excess is yours
questions.explanation: The above-cap carve-out and consent rights matter here.

questions.prompt: What's the most useful thing to do afterwards?
options: Post-mortem which terms actually decided the outcome
Remove indemnities from future deals
Renegotiate the cap on all old deals so this can't happen again next time
Switch every template to arbitration
questions.explanation: The only real feedback loop available.
